title: Living abroad but banking in India? Don’t let your Indian mobile number become a problem- Moneycontrol.com
text:
My Alerts Go Ad-Free Follow us on: 15                          Quick, easy & completely paperless. Your Indian SIM may still be linked to bank accounts, credit cards and investments. Keeping it active, checking roaming and setting up backup access can save you from getting locked out when you need an OTP   September 12, 2026 / 10:43 IST             When you move abroad, your Indian mobile number may seem like one of the easier things to leave behind. You have a new local number, most conversations happen on WhatsApp anyway, and the old SIM may spend months barely being used. Then you need to transfer money from an Indian bank account and the OTP doesn't arrive. For many NRIs, the Indian number registered with their bank remains important even years after they move overseas. It may be used for transaction OTPs, account alerts, credit cards and other financial services. The good news is that you can continue using an Indian mobile number abroad. The bigger question is whether you have set it up properly to keep working. Before leaving India, check whether international roaming is active on the number. Don't assume that because the SIM works in India it will automatically connect overseas. The requirements vary between telecom operators and can also depend on whether you have a prepaid or postpaid connection. You don't necessarily need to use your Indian SIM for calls and mobile data abroad. If its main purpose is receiving banking messages and OTPs, you may use a local SIM for everyday calls and data while keeping the Indian number active as a second SIM. But make sure you understand what your telecom operator requires to keep that number alive. A SIM that is barely used can eventually run into validity or inactivity problems. Recharge requirements and international roaming conditions differ between operators, so check the current rules for your plan. Losing the number altogether can be particularly troublesome if it is still registered with several banks and financial accounts. OTP delivery can also be unpredictable overseas. Your Indian operator has to connect through a foreign network, and messages can sometimes be delayed or fail to arrive. If an OTP isn't coming through, check whether the Indian SIM has connected to a local network and whether international roaming is active. Restarting the phone or manually selecting an available network may also help in some cases. Don't leave these checks until the day you need to make an urgent transaction. It is also worth asking your bank whether you can register your overseas mobile number. Many banks with NRI banking services allow customers to use international numbers for at least some services, particularly with NRE and NRO accounts. But the facilities are not identical across banks, and some transactions or services may still work differently with an overseas number. Check what your own bank supports rather than assuming an international number can replace your Indian one everywhere. Where available, set up other ways of accessing and authenticating your account too. Your bank's mobile app, net banking, email alerts and device-based authentication can provide useful alternatives or backups. Make sure your registered email address is current as well. The same housekeeping becomes even more important when you change phones or SIMs. If you are about to give up an Indian number, first make a list of everything connected to it. Bank accounts are the obvious place to start, but also check credit cards, demat and mutual fund accounts, insurance, tax accounts and any other financial service that may send an OTP to that number. Update them before the old number stops working. And don't forget security. An Indian SIM kept mainly for OTPs should still be protected carefully. If the phone or SIM is lost, contact the telecom operator quickly and inform your bank where necessary. For many NRIs, keeping an Indian number active is a relatively small expense compared with the inconvenience of suddenly losing access to an account from thousands of kilometres away. The simplest approach is to sort this out before you move: decide whether you will keep your Indian SIM, activate the services it needs overseas and check whether your bank can also use your foreign number. A little preparation can prevent an OTP from becoming a much bigger banking problem later.                        Discover the latest  Business News ,  Sensex , and  Nifty  updates.
